body_markdown:

Labor Day marks the unofficial end of summer and the final major travel weekend of the season. It also closes out the “100 Days of Summer,” the approximate 100-day period between Memorial Day and Labor Day, which is often associated with increased road safety risks.


Verra Mobility analyzed automated enforcement data from communities across the country to understand how driver behavior has changed during summer holiday weekends. Over the past several years, Labor Day speeding violations per camera have increased significantly, while red-light violations have risen moderately. However, data from Memorial Day and the Fourth of July 2026 offer a more encouraging signal as the final holiday weekend of summer approaches.


These trends come as new research suggests many drivers continue to view speeding differently from other risky driving behaviors. According to the AAA Foundation for Traffic Safety’s new report,[Attitudes Toward Speeding: Insights from Focus Groups and a National Survey of U.S. Drivers](https://aaafoundation.org/research/attitudes-toward-speeding-insights-from-focus-groups-and-a-national-survey-of-u-s-drivers/) , speeding is often viewed as a more acceptable unsafe driving behavior, with many drivers considering modest speeding acceptable even while acknowledging that posted speed limits are appropriate. That mindset may help explain why reducing speeds remains a persistent roadway safety challenge.


**Labor Day speeding reached a recent high in 2025**


Labor Day was the most stable of the three summer holiday weekends from 2023 through 2025, but speeding still moved sharply in the wrong direction last year. After declining in 2024, speed violations per camera increased by 45% in 2025, reaching the highest level of the three-year period.


High-speed violations, where drivers exceeded the posted limit by more than 20 mph, also rose. These violations increased 8%, reaching a three-year high in 2025. Although the increase was smaller than those recorded over Memorial Day and the Fourth of July, the continued upward movement showed that dangerous speeding remained a concern through the end of summer.


The timing of those violations also offers useful context. In 2025, speed violations per camera were highest on Saturday and lowest on Friday, suggesting risk may build after the holiday weekend begins rather than being present only during the initial departure period.


**Dangerous driving behaviors extended beyond speeding**


Red-light violations followed a similar pattern. After declining in 2024, violations per camera increased 11% in 2025. Labor Day was the only summer holiday weekend in 2025 when red-light violations exceeded the 2023 level.


Red-light violations per camera were highest on Friday and lowest on Monday. That pattern differs from speeding and reinforces that roadway risk can shift throughout a holiday weekend as traffic volumes and driver behavior change.


**Early summer trends offer reason for optimism**


So far, 2026 has looked notably different. Speed violations per camera declined over both Memorial Day and the Fourth of July compared with 2025, including an 87% decrease over the Fourth of July. Red-light violations per camera also fell across both holiday weekends.


The consistency of those declines across two different holiday weekends is encouraging. It may indicate that the sharp increases recorded in 2025 are beginning to ease. Still, two holiday periods do not establish a full-season trend, and Labor Day has its own travel patterns. In 2025, for example, Labor Day speeding increased less dramatically than Memorial Day or the Fourth of July, while red-light violations rose enough to surpass 2023 levels.


That makes Labor Day 2026 an important marker of violation trends. If the early-summer pattern continues, the holiday could close out the season with fewer violations per camera than last year.


**Drivers will determine how the summer ends**


The encouraging early-summer trends are a positive sign, but historical data also show how quickly progress can reverse: each major Labor Day metric declined or remained relatively stable in 2024, then increased in 2025. With speed contributing to[nearly one-third](https://www.nhtsa.gov/press-releases/trumps-transportation-department-reminds-drivers-that-speeding-catches-you?utm_source=chatgpt.com) of all traffic fatalities nationwide in 2024, drivers must take action to maintain the positive momentum seen earlier this summer and reduce their risk on the road.


To make this Labor Day weekend safe for everyone, follow posted speed limits, allow extra travel time, stay focused, and always come to a complete stop at red lights.
